title: The Geopolitics of Terrorism: The Case of China and Jammu & Kashmir
content:
Author : [Ayjaz Wani](https://www.orfonline.org/people-expert/ayjaz-wani)

# The Geopolitics of Terrorism: The Case of China and Jammu & Kashmir

China has historically facilitated Pakistan-sponsored terrorism in Jammu and Kashmir (J&K) not only through direct operational support but also by shielding Pakistan from global accountability. In the process, Beijing has protected its own geostrategic and geoeconomic interests in the region. This brief analyses China’s role in the persistent challenge of terrorism in J&K through direct and indirect support to Pakistani terror organisations and the state. It examines Beijing’s motivations for nurturing such an approach and underlines the imperatives for New Delhi.

**Attribution:**

Ayjaz Wani, “The Geopolitics of Terrorism: The Case of China and Jammu & Kashmir,” _ORF Issue Brief No. 889_, Observer Research Foundation, July 2026.

## Introduction

In April 2025, 26 individuals were killed in a terror attack by a Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT)-affiliated group in Pahalgam in Jammu and Kashmir (J&K). China was quick to condemn the attack and urged India and Pakistan to exercise restraint to maintain regional stability. [\[1\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn1) However, China has for years provided Pakistan with sustained diplomatic and material support, including indirectly backing Pakistan-sponsored terrorism in J&K. Beijing’s response to Pakistan-sponsored terrorism in J&K since 1989 has been characterised by a strategic alignment with Islamabad and efforts to restrain New Delhi’s influence globally. China has employed grey-zone strategies, combining political, economic, and military measures to aid India’s opponents and non-state actors, particularly in the Northeast region and J&K, by offering shelter, Chinese weapons, and tactical support to insurgents. [\[2\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn2)

The 1962 China-India war was pivotal in fostering closer cooperation between Beijing and Islamabad. Indeed, the strategic alignment between China and Pakistan strengthened in the 1960s, with Beijing becoming Islamabad's leading supplier of defence equipment, including technology and materials for the nuclear bomb, following the US suspension of military aid to Pakistan. [\[a\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_ftn1), [\[3\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn3)

In 1963, Pakistan illegally and unlawfully transferred parts of Indian territory (~ 42,735 sq km), including the Shaksgam Valley east of Hunza in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK), to China to strengthen diplomatic ties and “resolve” the border dispute. [\[4\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn4) This transfer of territory affected India’s traditional frontier along the Kunlun Range to the northwest of the Karakoram Pass; additionally, Beijing expanded its claim eastward along the Karakoram, including the Line of Actual Control (LAC). [\[5\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn5)

This border agreement also laid the groundwork for the construction of the Karakoram Highway, which was opened in 1978 by Chinese and Pakistani engineers to establish connectivity between China's Xinjiang province, a predominantly Muslim region in the northwest, and Pakistan, and facilitate trade, military logistics, and transit. However, the highway has also become a conduit for separatist and militant activities in Xinjiang. To contain insurgency in the province, China has strengthened ties with the Pakistani military, [\[6\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn6) courted terror outfits such as the Taliban, [\[7\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn7) and protected Pakistan-based terror groups such as the Jaish-e-Mohammed (JeM) and LeT at the United Nations Security Council (UNSC). [\[8\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn8)

Since 2008, amidst increased strategic alignment between China and Pakistan, Beijing has been issuing stapled visas to Indian passport holders from J&K and has also refused to grant visas to Indian army personnel posted in Kashmir. [\[9\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn9)

In 2008, a Chinese company was hired to develop the 969 MW Neelam-Jhelum hydropower project. The following year, Pakistan and China signed an agreement to start new projects in PoK, supported by a US$300-million line of credit from Beijing. [\[10\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn10) In 2015, China launched the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC)—a key project under its Belt and Road Initiative (BRI)—with an estimated investment of US$62 billion. CPEC focused on developing the Gwadar port, establishing a transportation network from Kashgar, and advancing energy projects and industrial cooperation. [\[11\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn11) Notably, India has consistently refused to join the BRI, as CPEC infringes on its sovereignty and integrity by passing through PoK, an issue it has repeatedly raised with China. [\[12\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn12)

Even as China-Pakistan ties deepen, Islamabad’s difficulties in ensuring the safety of Chinese workers highlight significant security shortcomings. [\[13\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn13) Terrorist organisations, such as the Balochistan Liberation Army, Tahreek-i-Taliban Pakistan, and Islamic State of Khorasan Province (ISKP), were involved in 14 terror attacks between 2021 and 2024 that resulted in the deaths of 20 Chinese nationals and injuries to 34 individuals. [\[14\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn14) The motive for the attacks was to sabotage CPEC and China’s economic and political footprint in the region. Pakistan’s inability to guarantee security was another factor in China’s decision to engage with the terror groups.

In August 2019, India abrogated Article 370 (which granted special status to the state of J&K) and Article 35A (which allowed J&K to define its permanent residents), dividing J&K into two union territories (J&K and Ladakh, which includes the Aksai Chin area that China claims as its own). The aim was to facilitate better administration, economic growth, and the region’s integration with the rest of the country. Notably, during the parliamentary debate on J&K bifurcation, the home minister stated that Aksai Chin and PoK are integral parts of India. [\[15\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn15) This statement alarmed China, prompting a response in the form of diplomatic protests, military measures, and administrative counteractions. [\[16\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn16) China challenged India’s sovereignty over Aksai Chin, reiterated Pakistan’s stance on solving the Kashmir issue according to the UNSC’s resolutions, and called for UN intervention. [\[17\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn17) Beijing also raised the issue at the UNSC in 2019, [\[18\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn18) although none of the other members expressed any reservation on India’s moves in J&K.

This brief analyses the China-Pakistan axis and instances of Beijing using grey-zone tactics, including economic, military, diplomatic, and political means, to enable terrorism in J&K.

## China’s Counterterrorism Policy and the Afghanistan-Pakistan Region

China’s counterterrorism strategy, in place since 1990, incorporates rigorous domestic security measures in the northwestern Xinjiang region. Additionally, China pursues regional diplomatic, military, and economic cooperation, particularly with Afghanistan and Pakistan which it considers vital partners in arresting the spillover of terrorist activities along its western borders and safeguarding regional infrastructure investments.

In the aftermath of Deng Xiaoping’s rise and the opening up of the economy in the late 1970s, China’s 1982 Constitution permitted the state to safeguard “normal religious activities” (Article 36). This provision granted Uyghurs cultural freedom and encouraged contact with Muslims abroad and travels to Islamic countries. [\[19\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn19)  The Chinese Communist Party reopened the Xinjiang Islamic Association, [\[b\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_ftn2) renovated mosques, and opened the Karakoram Highway, which facilitated the revival of religious practices rooted in the radical ideologies of the Jamaat-e-Islami (JeI) and Tablighi Jamat organisations from Pakistan. Many Uyghurs travelled to Pakistan for education or trade, where they were trained in _madrasas_(religious schools), and some returned with new political and religious ideas that influenced madrasas in Xinjiang. Additionally, traders and religious preachers from Pakistan began teaching at madrasas in Xinjiang, thereby increasing access to spiritual literature. Some Uyghurs were also trained in terror camps along the Afghanistan-Pakistan region, particularly the Balochistan province. [\[20\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn20) Additionally, the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan enabled the _mullahs_ (Muslim religious teachers, scholars, or leaders) to interpret _jihad_ (struggle/effort) in a way that motivated the people; consequently, some Uyghurs joined terror groups in Afghanistan, fighting for either the Northern Alliance or the Taliban. [\[21\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn21)

At the same time, the Uyghurs also faced socioeconomic alienation due to Han dominance in every social sphere, fuelling further ethnic discord among the indigenous Uyghurs. [\[22\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn22) Waves of protests against Chinese rule followed in 1980, 1981, 1985, and 1987, ultimately culminating in the Baren town incident in 1990, when some protestors, who had been trained in the Afghanistan-Pakistan region, used automatic weapons and grenades that caused severe damage to government property and resulted in injuries to many security personnel. The Chinese government deployed over a thousand troops who succeeded in eliminating the insurgents. However, reports indicate that approximately 60 civilians and eight security officers lost their lives. [\[23\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn23) In 1992 and 1993, there were increased attacks by Uyghur insurgents, and in 1997, on the day of Deng Xiaoping’s funeral, there were several bus bombings in Urumqi, the capital of Xinjiang. [\[24\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn24) Since then, China has cited separatism, extremism, and terrorism as the reasons for the cultural suppression of Uyghurs in Xinjiang. [\[25\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn25)

In Central Asia, where most Uyghur exiles now reside, Beijing has achieved its objective of suppressing the voice of Uyghur exiles living in the region through bilateral and multilateral platforms, such as the Shanghai Five, [\[c\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_ftn3) established in 1996 and which evolved into the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) in 2001. China has employed the SCO and bilateral agreements with Central Asian nations to suppress Uyghur organisations and Uyghurs residing in these countries. Since July 1998, the organisation has focused on collective efforts to combat separatism, extremism, and terrorism, mainly addressing Chinese concerns about Uyghur militants in Central Asia. Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan banned Uyghur organisations by 2006 and added them to terror lists. [\[26\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn26)

The increased unrest in Xinjiang and the rise in the number of Uyghurs joining terror groups in the Afghanistan-Pakistan region led China to develop a long-term plan to tackle instability at home and abroad. Beijing launched the domestic ‘Strike Hard’ campaign in 1997, which banned unofficial madrasas and led to the arrest of approximately 2,773 Uyghurs. [\[27\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn27) Authorities also seized 6,000 pounds of explosives and 31,000 rounds of ammunition. Uyghur sources claimed that over 57,000 Uyghurs were detained on flimsy charges by Chinese authorities. In 1997, Chinese authorities also built a fence along the 750-km border with Pakistan to limit external assistance to Uyghur militants in Xinjiang. [\[28\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn28) In 1999, Beijing protested to Islamabad after 16 Uyghur militants trained in Pakistan-based camps were arrested in Pakistan. [\[29\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn29)

In the 1990s, Chinese intelligence agencies also met with al-Qaeda leaders and asked them not to recruit Uyghurs. In 1997, al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden did not criticise China in his public statements, claiming that Muslims in Xinjiang were being blamed for US-sponsored blasts in the country. [\[30\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn30) However, in 1997, Hasan Mahsum, an Uyghur who had been imprisoned after the Baren incident, left China and formed the East Turkistan Islamic Movement (ETIM) in Afghanistan. Bin Laden pledged funds to ETIM in 1999, and the organisation became part of a network of terror groups in the Afghanistan-Pakistan region. [\[31\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn31)

In December 2000, Chinese Ambassador Lu Shulin met with Taliban leader Mullah Mohammad Omer and sought assurance that the group would not allow any anti-Chinese terrorist activity being launched from its territory. [\[32\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn32) Mahsum was killed by Pakistani security agencies in 2003, and Abdul Haq Turkestani became the leader of ETIM and eventually also a member of al-Qaeda’s executive council. [\[33\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn33) Haq was killed in North Waziristan in May 2010, but Pakistani security forces were hesitant to carry out large-scale operations in the Federally Administered Tribal Areas, where most ETIM members stayed. Notably, another point of hesitancy was that terrorists and terror groups in the Afghanistan-Pakistan region served as crucial assets and strategic instruments for Pakistan’s foreign policy.

## ‘War on Terror’ and China’s Double Standards

Amidst the North Atlantic Treaty Organization’s (NATO) invasion of Afghanistan to topple the Taliban government in the aftermath of the September 2001 terror attacks, China sought to shape the global narrative on human rights violations against Uyghurs in Xinjiang. China began lobbying against the Uyghurs at the UN, alongside the US and other Western countries. In 2002, Beijing released a white paper accusing Uyghur militants affiliated with ETIM of collaborating with al-Qaeda and the Taliban against China, and blaming ETIM for over 200 acts of terror in Xinjiang that had resulted in 162 deaths and 440 serious injuries. [\[34\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn34) In the same year, the US designated ETIM as a terrorist organisation to gain China's support at the UNSC for NATO’s military efforts in Afghanistan. This designation effectively justified stricter anti-Uyghur measures, such as increased surveillance, cultural suppression, and mass detention in Xinjiang, under the guise of counterterrorism. China also ensured the destruction of Uyghur camps in the Afghanistan-Pakistan region. [\[35\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn35)

After 2010, Chinese counterterrorism policy in the Afghanistan-Pakistan region evolved. China grew increasingly uneasy about the American presence on its western borders and perceived the US involvement in Afghanistan as a geostrategic threat. [\[36\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn36) Additionally, the Taliban revived with direct support and training from Pakistan. [\[37\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn37) Beijing again adopted a dual approach, maintaining cooperation with the Afghan government and the US, while quietly engaging with the Taliban through Pakistani intermediaries. In 2015, Chinese officials openly met with the Taliban in Urumqi with the assistance of Pakistani security agencies. [\[38\]](https://www.orfonline.org/research/the-geopolitics-of-terrorism-the-case-of-china-and-jammu-kashmir#_edn38)

# On Our Radar

On Our Radar scans conflicts and crises around the globe every week and features some of the hotspots Crisis Group’s analysts are closely watching. Whether an under-reported trend or a headline-grabbing development, our field experts explain why it matters or what should be done.

## 3 July 2026

[**AFGHANISTAN**](https://www.crisisgroup.org/asia-pacific/south-asia/afghanistan) **-** [**PAKISTAN**](https://www.crisisgroup.org/asia-pacific/south-asia/pakistan)  Tensions between Afghanistan and Pakistan flared again this week. On Sunday, Pakistani forces once again carried out strikes across the border in Afghanistan, saying they killed 29 militants. Islamabad said the strikes were retaliation for recent attacks inside Pakistan, including a Karachi assault that killed three security personnel. According to the UN, at least 28 civilians were killed and another 49 injured in the strikes. Pakistan accuses the Afghan Taliban of sheltering anti-Pakistan militants, which Taliban officials deny. On Wednesday, Afghanistan said it carried out strikes inside Pakistan, targeting ISIS and other armed opposition groups. Islamabad denies Taliban accusations of harbouring such groups and noted that it had intercepted four drones launched from Afghan territory. Crisis Group expert Ibraheem Bahiss says outside mediators should push the sides toward practical border and security arrangements before the cycle of strikes and counterstrikes escalates further.

[**NIGERIA**](https://www.crisisgroup.org/africa/west-africa/nigeria)  Violence is again escalating in north-western Nigeria. Long plagued by bandits who engage in mass kidnappings for ransom, pillage and extortion, the region is also now seeing increased jihadist activity. Together, bandit and jihadist attacks killed over 150 people in Katsina, Kebbi, Sokoto and Zamfara states in June, a notable uptick from previous months. On 28 May, Islamic State Sahel Province claimed what appears to be its first reported attacks in the region, in which eighteen soldiers and one police officer were killed in Kebbi and Sokoto states. Amid this escalation, on 20 June prominent bandit leader Bello Turji claimed responsibility for deadly attacks on troops and declared his group ready for either peace talks or prolonged war with the government. If the bandit and jihadist threats are not reined in, says Crisis Group expert Nnamdi Obasi, north-western Nigeria could become part of the wider belt of instability in the Sahel.

[**SUDAN**](https://www.crisisgroup.org/africa/horn-africa/sudan)  Fighting centred on El Obeid, North Kordofan’s state capital, has intensified in recent weeks as drone strikes increase and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) mobilise around the city, raising fears of encirclement and blockade. UN relief chief Tom Fletcher warned Tuesday that El Obeid risks becoming “another El Fasher”, referring to North Darfur’s capital, which endured a prolonged siege before falling to the RSF last October and suffering mass atrocities. Crisis Group expert Shewit Woldemichael says a siege of El Obeid would deepen the humanitarian crisis facing civilians, many of whom have already fled to the city from fighting elsewhere. Meanwhile, the increased use of drones against El Obeid could allow for sustained attacks through the now-beginning rainy season, when ground fighting has typically slowed.

## 26 June 2026

[**BOLIVIA**](https://www.crisisgroup.org/latin-america-caribbean/andes/bolivia) President Rodrigo Paz declared a state of exception starting Saturday after more than 50 days of protests triggered by a land reform law and planned austerity measures. Authorities say at least 37 people have been injured in clashes between demonstrators and police. The decree bans the protesters’ roadblocks that have paralysed commercial traffic, causing shortages of basic goods in the administrative capital La Paz, and (temporarily) allows the armed forces to assist police in reopening key routes. It does not, however, suspend fundamental rights, as is often the case with states of exception in Latin America. Before making the declaration, Paz had signed an agreement to “pacify” the country with the biggest trade union, the Bolivian Workers’ Central, which withdrew from the streets. Most of the roadblocks have vanished since the measure took effect. But Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says tensions remain high. The unrest could erupt anew if the government fails to deliver on socio-economic commitments it made to the union or if other groups involved in the protests, including campesinos and Indigenous people, decide to resume the pressure.

[**COLOMBIA**](https://www.crisisgroup.org/latin-america-caribbean/andes/colombia)  Right-wing Abelardo de la Espriella won Sunday’s presidential runoff by the thinnest margin in Colombian history, defeating Iván Cepeda, who had campaigned on continuing leftist President Gustavo Petro’s social reform agenda. De la Espriella styles himself as an outsider. Boasting of his ties to U.S. President Donald Trump, who endorsed him before the vote, he has vowed to take an iron-fist approach to organised crime, for instance pledging to bomb narco-traffickers and build mega-prisons. Many Colombians are ready for such measures, says Crisis Group expert Renata Segura, having become frustrated with Petro’s attempts to negotiate “total peace” with criminal and other armed groups. But, as the close vote shows, nearly half the electorate is equally concerned about de la Espriella’s promise to circumvent checks and balances in pursuit of quick fixes. To protect public safety, Colombia needs to balance crimefighting with efforts to plug the gaps in state services that criminal organisations exploit, including for recruitment. The new government should not disregard negotiations, which, if done the right way, have proven an effective tool for reducing violence in Colombia.

[**U.S.**](https://www.crisisgroup.org/united-states) **-** [**IRAN**](https://www.crisisgroup.org/middle-east-north-africa/gulf-and-arabian-peninsula/iran) U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed Wednesday that technical delegations from the U.S. and Iran will reconvene at the end of June to resume talks aimed at ending the conflict between the two countries. By the terms of the memorandum of understanding reached between the Trump administration and Tehran in Islamabad earlier this month, these working groups are tasked with negotiating the details leading to a “final deal”, including nuclear commitments by Iran and sanctions relief provisions by the U.S. Maintaining momentum in dialogue is critical, says Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez, as the two sides have put forward clashing interpretations of the parameters they agreed to in Pakistan. The negotiations have many moving parts – related to the Strait of Hormuz and Lebanon, among other issues. In this ambitious scope lies promise, but also peril, as a setback on any one front could derail the whole endeavour.

## 19 June 2026

[**HAITI**](https://www.crisisgroup.org/latin-america-caribbean/caribbean/haiti) Visiting Tuesday, UN Secretary-General António Guterres said Haiti is suffering “the worst humanitarian crisis in the Western Hemisphere”. He toured the headquarters of the new Gang Suppression Force assembled to battle the criminal bands bedevilling the country. The UN released figures showing that gang violence has killed 2,300 people in the year to date and displaced a record 1.5 million more. Gangs have also kidnapped around 100 Haitians, including the defence ministry’s cabinet director last week. Crisis Group expert Diego Da Rin says much hope rests on the new force, but whether it can deliver remains to be seen as it builds toward its mandated strength of 5,500. Gangs, meanwhile, appear to be adapting, attacking senior officials and expanding abductions into formerly safe areas, possibly to deter anti-gang operations where kidnapping victims are held.

[**MYANMAR**](https://www.crisisgroup.org/asia-pacific/south-east-asia/myanmar) **-** [**CHINA**](https://www.crisisgroup.org/asia-pacific/north-east-asia/china)  Chinese President Xi Jinping hosted Myanmar’s coup-leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing on a state visit to Beijing this week. The two sides reaffirmed their “community with a shared future” and signed eighteen agreements covering areas including transport and development. The visit highlighted Beijing’s priorities in Myanmar: border stability, protection of Chinese investment, progress on select China-Myanmar Economic Corridor projects and continued cooperation in combating online scams and other transnational crime. Crisis Group expert Richard Horsey says the state visit’s symbolism may matter more than any individual deal, as it provides Min Aung Hlaing with a measure of the international legitimacy he craves. For China, meanwhile, it is an opportunity to lock in a dependency that provides growing strategic opportunities, while it pushes for greater calm in conflict-affected areas along the Myanmar border.

[**UKRAINE**](https://www.crisisgroup.org/europe/eastern-europe/ukraine) **-** [**RUSSIA**](https://www.crisisgroup.org/europe/caucasus/russia)  Overnight into Thursday, Ukraine launched its largest drone assault on Moscow since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, hitting an oil refinery and injuring at least seventeen people. Russia said it intercepted 194 drones around Moscow and nearly 1,000 drones and several cruise missiles nationwide over 24 hours. Ukraine said the attack was a response to Russian strikes earlier this week that damaged the UNESCO-listed Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra monastery. Moscow warned it would respond forcefully. Crisis Group expert Lucian Kim says the attacks highlight Ukraine’s efforts to demonstrate it can hit targets far inside Russia using deep-strike drones. But while such attacks create headlines, they have yet to affect the Kremlin’s warfighting ability and may harden support for the war among the Russian public.

## 12 June 2026

[**AFGHANISTAN**](https://www.crisisgroup.org/asia-pacific/south-asia/afghanistan) **-** [**PAKISTAN**](https://www.crisisgroup.org/asia-pacific/south-asia/pakistan)  Pakistan launched air raids Wednesday across the border with Afghanistan, killing 26 Pakistani Taliban fighters, according to Pakistani Information Minister Attaullah Tarar. The Afghan authorities, however, said the strikes killed thirteen people, including eleven children. The air raids came one day after Pakistani Taliban fighters ambushed a security outpost in Pakistan’s north west, killing six officers. These incidents ended a month of calm in the conflict between the two countries. Crisis Group expert Ibraheem Bahiss says violent flare-ups like these are likely to persist as long as both countries’ security concerns remain unaddressed.

[**IRAN**](https://www.crisisgroup.org/middle-east-north-africa/gulf-and-arabian-peninsula/iran) **-** [**U.S.**](https://www.crisisgroup.org/united-states) The fragile April ceasefire between Washington and Tehran wobbled as the two sides engaged in increasingly sharp exchanges of fire. U.S. forces launched repeated strikes on Iranian targets as Tehran retaliated by targeting U.S. bases in Bahrain, Jordan and Kuwait; Iran and Israel also traded blows for the first time in two months. On Thursday, U.S. President Donald Trump threatened that the U.S. would take control of Kharg island, site of Iran’s main oil terminals, and other energy infrastructure. He backtracked later in the day, cancelling new strikes and insisting that a negotiated deal with Tehran was close. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says an agreement would be welcome if it steadies the shaky truce and gives Washington and Tehran a clear path to future negotiations. Those talks are likely to be fraught, however, and may not guarantee the end of hostilities if certain issues remain unresolved, such as Israel’s continued attacks on and occupation of over 20 per cent of Lebanon.

[**WESTERN SAHARA**](https://www.crisisgroup.org/middle-east-north-africa/north-africa/western-sahara)  A Moroccan airstrike on Sunday killed three Polisario Front members who were carrying out an attack on Moroccan fortifications in Western Sahara. Among the dead was Lehbib Mohamed Abdelaziz, son of Polisario’s former secretary general, who had been rumoured to be a candidate to become the Front’s leader. His death marks a major loss for the Polisario. The Moroccan strike came as UN envoy Staffan De Mistura was visiting the Tindouf refugee camps for consultations with the Polisario. Crisis Group expert Riccardo Fabiani says this latest episode shows that negotiations to resolve the Western Sahara conflict are under increasing strain. The Polisario and its ally Algeria have routinely rejected framework agreements based on Morocco’s autonomy plan as other deadly attacks have eroded trust between the parties.

## 5 June 2026

[**COLOMBIA**](https://www.crisisgroup.org/latin-america-caribbean/andes/colombia) Far-right presidential candidate Abelardo de la Espriella won a first-round victory in the 31 May elections, setting up a 21 June run-off against left-wing senator Iván Cepeda. Cepeda promises to reduce inequality and continue talks with armed groups, while de la Espriella advocates iron-fist policies, including bombing organised crime groups, building mega-jails and restoring traditional values. After the vote, President Gustavo Petro alleged irregularities, despite international observers calling the vote transparent, while U.S. President Donald Trump openly backed de la Espriella. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says Petro’s claims raise concerns over a peaceful transfer of power if Cepeda loses, while Trump’s involvement has fuelled resentment over foreign interference, which could further trigger demonstrations. The run-off could also test whether Trump’s endorsement helps or hurts candidates elsewhere in the region.

[**CONFLICT-RELATED SEXUAL VIOLENCE**](https://www.crisisgroup.org/gender-and-conflict)  The UN on 29 May released its annual report on conflict-related sexual violence, showing that reported cases more than doubled in 2025 after rising 25 per cent the year before. UN Women also recently reported that in Sudan alone, the number of women and girls needing support after sexual violence has quadrupled since civil war broke out three years ago. Crisis Group expert Cristal Downing says survivor services are increasingly scarce after major U.S. aid cuts in 2025 hit programming for which Washington had been the largest donor. Compounding the problem, Washington’s February 2026 “Protecting Human Flourishing in Foreign Assistance” policy restricts aid recipients’ work and speech on abortion. Though the policy’s ban on “promoting” abortion exempts cases of rape, many NGOs fear inconsistent enforcement and unclear compliance requirements, leaving them to choose between U.S. conditions that may limit post-rape care and refusing funding at the risk of jeopardising their wider operations.

[**LEBANON**](https://www.crisisgroup.org/middle-east-north-africa/east-mediterranean-mena/lebanon)  Israel and Lebanon on Wednesday agreed to a new U.S.-brokered ceasefire deal, which would establish pilot zones in southern Lebanon where Hizbollah operatives would be barred. The deal follows a severe Israeli escalation, including its deepest incursion into Lebanese territory in 26 years, which threatened to upset ongoing U.S.-Iran talks. The ceasefire depends on Hizbollah halting attacks and withdrawing fighters from south of the Litani River to allow the Lebanese army to assume control there. On Thursday, Hizbollah rejected the terms, after Israel said it would continue military operations for now. Crisis Group expert David Wood says the “pilot zones” proposal could offer a pragmatic way to address the parties’ security concerns. Unless Israel and Hizbollah both cease fire, however, this latest agreement will soon collapse entirely.

## 29 May 2026

[**GAZA**](https://www.crisisgroup.org/middle-east-north-africa/east-mediterranean-mena/israelpalestine) Nickolay Mladenov, the Bulgarian diplomat tasked by the U.S.-designed Board of Peace with overseeing the Gaza ceasefire, briefed the UN Security Council last week on his team’s first six months of work. He was upbeat, releasing a fifteen-point “roadmap” for the next stage. But conditions remain dire on the ground. Israel’s siege is tightening, meaning that reconstruction is impossible. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Friday he has ordered the Israeli army to increase the proportion of Gaza it controls from 60 to 70 per cent, in effect squeezing the strip’s two million people into an even tighter corner. Israeli airstrikes have taken more than 900 Palestinian lives during the ceasefire, including the commander of Hamas’s armed wing and, only days later, his successor, who was killed Wednesday along with his family. Israeli media reported that the Board of Peace had “approved” the assassinations. Crisis Group expert Max Rodenbeck says the Board’s strategy of making relief for Gaza’s people, whether humanitarian aid or broader hopes for the future, conditional on Hamas’s willingness to surrender its arms is deeply troubling and a recipe for prolonging their misery.

[**KOREAN PENINSULA**](https://www.crisisgroup.org/asia-pacific/north-east-asia/korean-peninsula)  Pyongyang said it tested two new missiles Tuesday, including a short-range, nuclear-capable cruise missile that it plans to deploy with troops facing South Korean soldiers across the Korean peninsula’s demilitarised zone. The same day, Seoul said it had also detected North Korean missile launches toward waters off the peninsula’s western coast. Crisis Group expert Chris Green says the advanced weapon tests will deepen the freeze in peninsular relations, with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un branding South Korea his country’s foremost enemy and pledging to make the border “an impregnable fortress”. Along with Pyongyang’s growing closeness to Moscow and questions about Washington’s commitment to defending South Korea amid its mounting competition with Beijing, the tests are likely to bolster the consensus in Seoul behind more intensive military modernisation of its own.

[**MALI**](https://www.crisisgroup.org/africa/sahel/mali) As many as 50 people were killed Wednesday in jihadist raids on two villages in the central Mopti region, underscoring the breadth of the threat posed by the al-Qaeda affiliate Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM). Meanwhile, JNIM continued to enforce a partial siege of the capital Bamako, preventing scores of trucks bearing fuel and other supplies from reaching the city. title: China, India-linked hacking groups targeted Pakistani law enforcement, report says
content:
July 9 (Reuters) - Multiple Pakistani law enforcement agencies were targeted in separate hacking campaigns linked to groups associated with China and India, researchers at cybersecurity firm SentinelOne said on Thursday.

The campaigns offer a glimpse into foreign efforts to gather information on Pakistan's security challenges including militant violence, tensions with Afghanistan and the country's economic collaboration with China.

"When multiple cyberespionage actors operate against law enforcement institutions of a single state, the convergence itself is a signal of target value," Aleksandar Milenkoski, a principal threat researcher at SentinelOne, wrote in a blog published on Thursday.

"What draws them is a particular kind of institution: one that holds the government's internal security picture, what it knows about the threats inside its borders, and how it acts against them."

SentinelOne said it found evidence of multiple hacking campaigns and intrusions carried out by Chinese- and Indian-linked hacking groups between February 2024 and April 2026, most notably against the Balochistan police, which serves Pakistan's southwestern province of the same name.

Liu Chang, the spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, said in an emailed statement that China "firmly opposes and combats all forms of cyberattacks in accordance with the law, and does not allow any country or individual to engage in such illegal activities within China's territory or by using China's infrastructure."

The Indian Embassy in Washington did not provide an answer to questions about the analysis.

The report said Chinese interest in the agencies could be linked to the safety of Chinese nationals working in Pakistan, who have been targeted in deadly attacks in recent years. Interest from groups linked to India could be related to tensions between the two countries and Pakistan's broader security posture, it said.

According to Milenkoski, the operations targeting the Balochistan police involved network equipment, web servers and several online applications, including the force's Complaint Management System.

The Balochistan police did not respond to a request for comment.

Other targets included the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa police, the Islamabad police and the Punjab Safe Cities Authority (PSCA), an autonomous government agency that operates systems used by the police in major cities in Punjab province.

The Khyber Pakhtunkhwa police said in a statement that security of its systems is "a matter of the highest priority," and that "there is no evidence that any core KP police system, network, or critical application has been successfully compromised."

"It is pertinent to mention that during the heightened Pakistan-India tensions last year, KP Police experienced an increase in attempted cyber activities," the agency said, and that in "one isolated incident, the login credentials of an end user were compromised."

The Islamabad Police, PSCA, and Pakistani Ministry of Interior did not respond to a request for comment.

Reporting by AJ Vicens in Detroit. Additional reporting by Mushtaq Ali in Peshawar; Editing by Sanjeev Miglani
query: China India linked hacking groups Pakistani law enforcement

title: Sri Lanka seeks six suspects in Chinese national's murder linked to cybercrimes
content:
COLOMBO, July 30 - Sri Lankan police are searching for six people regarding the murder of a Chinese national suspected of links to computer-related scams, an official said on Thursday, in a crackdown on cyberscam centres tied to transnational fraud networks.

Authorities have arrested about 700 foreign nationals this year, Indian, Chinese, Nepalis and Vietnamese among them, or nearly double the 2025 figure, from hotels, rented houses and apartments nationwide, police data showed.

Police believe the Chinese national, whose body was retrieved a week ago from the town of Eheliyagoda, about 60 km from Colombo, was abducted in the island nation's commercial capital.

"Three suspects linked to the murder are believed to be in Sri Lanka and we have imposed a travel ban on them," police spokesman Frederick Wootler told Reuters.

"Three suspects who managed to leave the country are being traced with support from Interpol."

Two Chinese nationals linked to the murder have been arrested and will be presented in court on August 4, he added, while declining to reveal the identity of the victim.

He is suspected to be part of a larger group of Chinese nationals linked to computer-related scams, two police sources told Reuters, speaking on condition of anonymity.

The Chinese foreign ministry and the Chinese embassy in Colombo did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The nationwide raids turned up hundreds of mobile telephones, laptops and desktop computers, leading authorities to suspect the foreign nationals had ties to cybercrime networks, they said.

Most of those arrested appeared in court before being deported for overstaying their visas or for working on tourist visas.

Reporting by Uditha Jayasinghe; Editing by Clarence Fernandez
query: Sri Lanka Chinese national murder cybercrimes

title: Central Asia Is Increasingly Looking Beyond Iran
content:
WASHINGTON -- The recent military escalation between the US and Iran may have subsided for now, but the geopolitical consequences are only beginning to unfold.

As uncertainty hangs over the Strait of Hormuz and regional security, governments across Central Asia are quietly rethinking decades of strategic assumptions about trade, connectivity, and access to global markets.

Ken Moriyasu, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute focusing on Eurasian affairs, has just returned from Central Asia, where he says one message stood out above all others: countries that once viewed Iran as their natural gateway to the sea are increasingly looking elsewhere.

Earlier this year, after the conflict in February, there were discussions at think tanks around March where Central Asian ambassadors spoke about the possibilities if stability returned to Iran.

If Iran moved toward a pro-business administration, they argued, it would provide the shortest route to warm-water ports for Central Asian countries. There was considerable optimism about what could happen if Iran became stable.

But on this trip, it became very clear to me that Central Asian countries are moving away from that option. They are talking much more about Pakistan and Afghanistan -- using Afghanistan as a transit route to Pakistan.

Even though Afghanistan and Pakistan have their own tensions, they believe resolving those issues is more realistic than waiting for regime change in Iran or for a level of stability that would convince Israel to stop attacking Iran. For them, that now appears to be a very distant possibility.

So, they are looking first at Afghanistan, and if that does not work, then at the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC). On paper, CPEC is a fantastic idea. In reality, it has not progressed as much as expected. But even so, Central Asian countries believe a China-Pakistan connection is still more achievable than waiting for circumstances inside Iran to improve.

Pakistan is unique because of its geography. It is both a continental country and a maritime country.

That is very different from India. India is effectively separated from Eurasia by the Himalayas and by Pakistan. It does not really have direct access to Central Asia.

Pakistan is different. It has direct access to Central Asia while also possessing major ports at Karachi and Gwadar that connect to the sea.

Field Marshal Asim Munir (Pakistan's powerful army chief) also has a good relationship with US President Donald Trump. President Trump has recognized that and has clearly decided to lean on Pakistan -- not only for mediation involving Iran, but also because he sees Pakistan as a crucial partner in the broader strategic competition across Eurasia involving China and Russia.

What's interesting is how Pakistan is playing this. Pakistan is engaging more with the United States, but that does not mean it is shifting away from China. It is very important for Americans to understand that by engaging more closely with Washington, Pakistan is actually encouraging China to become even more committed to the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor.

Pakistan is using both sides, and it is working.

A good example is Kazakhstan. Its main oil export pipeline to the Black Sea has effectively been disrupted because of drone attacks, most likely linked to Ukraine's campaign against Russian infrastructure. Around 80 percent of Kazakhstan's oil exports normally move through the Black Sea.

Kazakhstan has two alternatives. One is the Middle Corridor through the Caspian Sea to Azerbaijan. The other is the existing pipeline to China.

Although Kazakhstan would prefer the Middle Corridor, oil must first be transported by tanker across the Caspian Sea to Baku, which limits capacity.

The quickest solution is simply to send more oil to China, and I think that is what will happen.

So, despite Central Asia's concerns about becoming overly dependent on China, that dependence is increasing unless countries such as the United States and Japan invest in Caspian infrastructure that would expand oil shipments between Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan.

From Tehran's perspective, could losing Central Asia become Iran's biggest strategic setback since sanctions were imposed?

Yes. Iran is desperate not to lose this war, but through its own actions it is losing Central Asia. At the same time, it is not only Iran that is pushing Central Asia away. US policy is also contributing.

For example, there have been attacks around Chabahar, the southern Iranian port where India has invested to create an alternative to Gwadar. Those developments make it much harder for an Iran-based trade corridor to compete with the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor.

So, this is partly Iran's responsibility, but it is also a consequence of US policy. Together, they are making the Iran route far less relevant.
query: Central Asia looking beyond Iran Afghanistan Pakistan China corridor

title: Expanding the neighborhood: China's widening and deepening involvement in South Asia and the Gulf states
content:
Chinese investments, trade relations, diplomatic overtures, and geopolitical penetration of the Gulf and South Asia are broadly altering the economic and political landscapes of local countries. Notable developments like the Chinese-brokered Saudi Arabia-Iran agreement signed in March 2023, the roughly $300 billion economic and security pact China reached with Iran in 2021, and ongoing work on the $65 billion China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) have all reshaped strategic thinking across the region.

MEI cordially invites you to an expert panel that will examine the growing multifaceted impact of Beijing's outreach to the wider Middle East -- namely the countries of the Gulf and South Asia. In what ways did Pakistan's close relations and economic dependency on China influence its reaction to the growing Chinese involvement with Saudi Arabia and Iran? What has a more regionally engaged China meant for Afghanistan's Taliban government? And how has India, with its expanding economic links to Arab countries and Iran as well as long-running defense ties with Russia, reacted to increased Chinese involvement in all those key partners?

Speakers:
- Yun Sun, Senior Fellow and Co-Director, China, East Asia, Stimson Center
- Daniel Markey, Senior Advisor, South Asia Programs, USIP
- Khaled Almaeena, Fmr. Editor-in-Chief, Arab News; Saudi Gazette
- Syed Mohammad Ali, Non-Resident Scholar, Middle East Institute
- Gerald M. Feierstein (moderator), Distinguished Senior Fellow on U.S. Diplomacy; Director, Arabian Peninsula Program, Middle East Institute

Key themes: China's geopolitical penetration of South Asia and the Gulf; the Saudi-Iran detente brokered by Beijing; the $65 billion CPEC and its reshaping of Pakistan's strategic calculus; China's engagement with the Taliban-led government in Afghanistan; India's response to deepening Chinese involvement across its key regional partners; implications for U.S. strategic and security interests.
query: China's widening involvement South Asia Gulf states Pakistan Afghanistan

title: A Distracted Pakistan: Strategic Opportunity In The Afghanistan-Pakistan War
content:
Background

Tensions between Pakistan and the Taliban-led government of Afghanistan, simmering since the Taliban's return to power in August 2021, escalated into open warfare in late February 2026. Following weeks of militant attacks inside Pakistan, the Pakistan Air Force struck alleged Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and Islamic State-Khorasan camps in Afghanistan's Nangarhar, Paktika and Khost provinces on 21 February, prompting Taliban retaliatory attacks on Pakistani border posts on 26 February. Pakistan's Defence Minister, Khawaja Asif, declared an "open war" and launched Operation Ghazab lil-Haq, a large-scale campaign of air and ground strikes across eastern Afghanistan.

An earlier round of hostilities in October 2025 had produced a Qatar- and Turkey-mediated ceasefire that proved short-lived, with follow-up talks in Doha and Istanbul collapsing before the February 2026 escalation. A subsequent Eid al-Fitr truce in March 2026, and Chinese-mediated talks in Urumqi in April 2026, each produced only temporary lulls, with tensions resurfacing by June 2026 amid renewed Pakistani air and drone strikes and Afghan retaliatory action in Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Pakistani strikes in late June 2026 reportedly killed 36 Afghan civilians, drawing condemnation from Kabul and a formal statement from India's Ministry of External Affairs.

United Nations human rights experts have characterised Pakistan's cross-border strikes as a violation of the prohibition on the use of force under the UN Charter, while noting that Pakistan has not established that the Taliban directed or controlled TTP attacks on its territory. The conflict has thus evolved from periodic border skirmishes into a sustained, multi-front crisis that has consumed significant Pakistani military, diplomatic and economic bandwidth through mid-2026.

Functioning

The Af-Pak war functions as a genuine two-front strategic dilemma for Pakistan's security establishment. Pakistani forces have simultaneously had to conduct sustained air operations across the western border, defend against Taliban and TTP retaliatory strikes and drone incursions into Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and respond to a wave of domestic terrorist attacks, including a suicide bombing at a Shia mosque in Islamabad and an attack on a security post in Bajaur. Pakistan has pursued a strategy of establishing forward "buffer zones" inside Afghan territory along the Durand Line, seeking to hold seized pockets as leverage in future negotiations.

Diplomatically, Pakistan has been drawn into successive rounds of externally mediated negotiations, in Doha, Istanbul and Urumqi, each consuming senior political and military attention without producing a durable settlement. Economically, the near-total closure of the border has halted bilateral trade and disrupted the Afghanistan-Pakistan Transit Trade Agreement framework, compounding pre-existing economic strain in both countries. Collectively, these military, diplomatic and economic burdens constitute a significant distraction, diverting Pakistani strategic attention and resources away from its eastern frontier with India at a time of already heightened India-Pakistan tensions following their brief conflict in 2025.

Impact

Pakistan's preoccupation with its western front has opened a clear strategic window for India, even though New Delhi continues to frame its engagement primarily in terms of development and humanitarian support rather than explicit geopolitics. Analysts observe that Pakistani airstrikes inside Afghan territory have inadvertently nudged Kabul closer to India, forged around a shared concern over Islamabad's aggressive posture.

Evidence of Growing Indian Influence in Kabul: Afghan ministers, including the Foreign, Health, Commerce, and Agriculture Ministers, have undertaken official visits to New Delhi. During his 2026 visit, Afghan Agriculture Minister Mawlawi Ataullah Omari publicly emphasised shared civilisational ties, while Kabul actively pitched for easier business access, visa relaxations, and long-term Indian infrastructure investments in mining and pharmaceuticals. In the FY 2026-27 Union Budget, India increased its direct development assistance to Afghanistan by 27% (to Rs 150 crore). In exchange for stepped-up health and agricultural aid, Kabul provided assurances that Afghan territory will not be used by hostile groups against India.

Evidence of Pakistan's Waning Leverage: Afghanistan-Pakistan bilateral transit trade plummeted from nearly $5 billion in FY21 to just $367 million in FY26. Kabul has increasingly replaced Pakistani goods and pharmaceuticals with imports from India and Iran, and activated the Air Freight Corridor (Kabul-Delhi and Kabul-Amritsar) and expanded utilisation of Iran's Chabahar Port, paired with the Zaranj-Delaram Highway, thereby bypassing Pakistani transit entirely.

China's Competing Mediation Role: Beijing's hosting of the Urumqi talks and its role as the sole penholder on Afghanistan at the UN Security Council give China parallel, and potentially competing, influence over any eventual Afghanistan-Pakistan settlement.

Way Forward

India's approach should continue to prioritise humanitarian and developmental engagement with Afghanistan, capacity-building, medical and food aid, and connectivity investment via Chabahar, over any overt strategic messaging that could be construed as exploiting Pakistan-Afghanistan hostilities, thereby preserving deniability while still gaining goodwill in Kabul. Continued, calibrated condemnation of civilian harm on both sides of the Durand Line, consistent with India's stated commitment to Afghan sovereignty and territorial integrity, allows New Delhi to occupy a principled position without being drawn into direct entanglement in the conflict.
